summary: Defines the Segment Routing Header (SRH), a new IPv6 routing extension header used to apply Segment Routing to the IPv6 data plane. It describes the header and how SR-capable nodes process it to steer packets along a list of segments.

plainLanguage.summary: The Segment Routing Header (SRH) carries a list of IPv6 segments that direct a packet through a network. This RFC defines the header fields, optional TLVs, and how source, transit, and endpoint nodes process the packet.

subtitle: How IPv6 carries an ordered segment list and processes it at each segment endpoint.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 needs a packet format for its segment list and rules for nodes that process each segment.
tldr.mechanism: The Segment Routing Header carries a reversed list of 128-bit IPv6 addresses and a Segments Left counter. Each endpoint updates the destination address to the next segment.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8754 is a Proposed Standard that defines the SRH and its processing. It is updated by RFC 9800.

today: RFC 8754 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020. It is updated by RFC 9800.

sections.title: Segment Routing over IPv6
sections.content:
Segment Routing can use the IPv6 data plane. RFC 8754 defines a new IPv6 routing extension header, the Segment Routing Header (SRH), and specifies how Segment Routing-capable nodes process it.

In SRv6, a Segment Identifier (SID) is an IPv6 address. The current segment is in the packet's destination address. A source node creates or encapsulates the packet, a transit node forwards it using IPv6 routing, and a segment endpoint processes a locally assigned segment.
sections.plainLanguage: The SRH gives an IPv6 packet an ordered route through segment endpoints. Ordinary transit routers forward toward the current destination without processing the SRH.

sections.title: Fields in the SRH
sections.content:
The SRH uses Routing Type 4. Its fields include the IPv6 Next Header and Header Extension Length, Routing Type, Segments Left, Last Entry, Flags, Tag, the Segment List, and optional Type Length Value (TLV) objects. Each Segment List entry is a 128-bit IPv6 address.

The list is encoded in reverse order: entry zero is the final segment, and the highest-index entry is the first. Last Entry gives the zero-based index of the last entry. Segments Left changes as the packet advances. The defined flag bits must be zero when sent, and the Tag may identify a packet class or group.
sections.plainLanguage: The SRH stores IPv6 segment addresses in reverse order. A counter identifies which segment is active, and the endpoint updates that counter as the packet moves.

sections.title: Padding and HMAC TLVs
sections.content:
Optional Type Length Value (TLV) objects follow the Segment List. An unknown TLV type must be ignored, and a TLV that extends beyond the SRH causes an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Parameter Problem and packet discard. Padding TLVs align later TLVs or make the SRH a multiple of 8 octets; implementations that add or parse TLVs must support padding.

The optional Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) TLV lets a configured endpoint check that an authorized party selected the SRH and that the Segment List was not changed. Its 4-octet Key ID identifies a pre-shared key and algorithm, and the HMAC is at most 32 octets. An implementation supporting this function must implement SHA-256. Key selection and distribution are outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding TLVs align the header. An optional HMAC TLV lets a configured node check the source and segment list using a shared key.

sections.title: How Sources and Endpoints Process Packets
sections.content:
A source sets the IPv6 destination to the first segment and writes the remaining segments into the SRH. It sets Segments Left and Last Entry based on the list length. If a policy has one segment and needs no SRH information, the source may omit the SRH. A reduced SRH omits the first segment because it is already in the IPv6 destination address.

A transit node must not inspect the routing header; it forwards toward the IPv6 destination. When an endpoint processes an SRH with Segments Left above zero, it checks the list bounds, decrements the counter, copies the next address into the IPv6 destination, decrements Hop Limit, and resubmits the packet. Invalid fields or an expired Hop Limit cause the specified ICMP error and packet discard.
sections.plainLanguage: The source sets the first destination and includes the remaining segments in the SRH. At an endpoint, the node selects the next address from the list and forwards the packet again.

sections.title: Deployment Inside an SR Domain
sections.content:
The deployment model in this RFC uses SIDs within an SR domain and for that domain's packets. Edge nodes drop packets arriving from outside when their destination is in the domain's SID block. Each endpoint also filters packets to its local SIDs when the source is outside the domain.

The RFC recommends a larger Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) inside the domain to account for encapsulation. It requires a flow label on interdomain packets and requires transit and endpoint nodes to use that label for equal-cost multipath (ECMP) hashing. A host may add an SRH and a trusted router or switch may verify its HMAC before the packet enters the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering at the domain edge and at each endpoint prevents outside packets from directly using its SIDs. The SRH is not encrypted, so it does not hide the segment list from observers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 8754 treats the SR domain as trusted and requires filtering to restrict access to its SIDs. It recommends filtering IPv6 source addresses as well. The HMAC TLV can check that the list was not modified, but compromised nodes inside the domain can still attack it.

The SRH is unencrypted and may reveal intermediate SIDs, topology, traffic flows, or service use to someone who can observe packets in the domain. ICMP error generation can be abused, and the RFC relies on ICMPv6 rate limiting to address that risk. It does not define use of the SRH with the IP Authentication Header.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering controls who can send packets to domain SIDs, and HMAC can protect the segment list from changes. The SRH itself is not secret, and an attacker inside the trusted domain may still cause harm.

fields.desc: Identifies the header after the SRH.

fields.name: Segments Left
fields.desc: Counter updated as the packet advances.

fields.name: Last Entry
fields.desc: Zero-based index of the final list entry.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Unused flags are zero on transmission.

fields.name: Tag
fields.desc: Can identify a packet class or group.

fields.name: Segment List entry
fields.desc: An IPv6 address; the list stores the final segment first.
